items.prompt: Who are the customers of an internal platform team?
choices: Other engineering teams inside the company
The company's paying end users on the public site
Only the executives who originally funded the team
items.explanation: A platform serves the teams that build on it.

items.prompt: A script hardcodes one team's repository layout. Why does it fail as a platform?
choices: It is written in a language few teams know
It assumes one team's setup is universal
It runs too slowly for most other teams
items.explanation: A platform starts from what teams share, not from one team's quirks.

items.prompt: What does self-service mean for a deploy path?
choices: A team writes its own pipeline tool from scratch
A team asks the platform team through chat
A team deploys with no ticket
items.explanation: Self-service removes the human from the critical path.

items.prompt: Hiring more people to answer onboarding tickets mostly does what?
choices: Moves the bottleneck without removing it
Makes every team adopt the platform sooner
Removes the bottleneck for good
items.explanation: Every first deploy still waits on a person.

items.prompt: Which sign points to a platform rather than a product?
choices: A platform engineer attends every single deploy
Each new team follows one documented path
Each new team gets a bespoke setup
items.explanation: A shared documented path is the platform signature.

items.prompt: Why treat adoption as something to measure?
choices: It lets the platform team bill other teams monthly
It proves that the template code compiles cleanly
It shows whether teams choose the road
items.explanation: Customers who do not adopt a product have told you something.

items.prompt: A platform team spends most of its week on onboarding calls. What does that suggest?
choices: The platform is not yet self-service
The team should write more documentation tickets
The platform is working as intended
items.explanation: Heavy hand-holding means the path is not reusable yet.

items.prompt: What does a ticket put on every team's critical path?
choices: The security team's weekly calendar
The platform team's headcount
The cloud provider's published uptime
items.explanation: Each ticket waits for the platform team's capacity.

items.prompt: Team A's deploy tool is used by the one team that asked and needs a platform engineer for each integration. Team B's tool is used by 20 teams with nobody from the platform team present. Which is operating as a platform, and why?
choices: Neither, because a platform needs a public user interface first
Team B, because adoption happens without its builders present
Team A, because tailored help gives better results for each team
Both, because each tool deploys software successfully for someone
items.explanation: Reuse without hand-holding is the test. Both deploy software, so successful deploys cannot tell them apart.
items.reference:
Product versus platform
product: solves one customer's problem
platform: solves the whole class of problem
customer: other engineering teams
test: do teams adopt it without the platform team present?
Why: a platform is judged by reuse without hand-holding, not by whether the first deploy worked.
items.learnMore:
Platform versus product

A script tuned to one team's layout works for that team and fails the rest. Extracting what every team shares, and parameterizing only what truly varies, is the step that turns a one-off into a platform.

Common mistake

Counting a tool as a platform because it works. Working once says nothing about whether a second team can use it alone.
items.reflection: Think of something you built for one person that others later asked to borrow. What would you have had to change so they could use it without you?

items.prompt: A platform team is asked whether it should add two engineers to clear a 60-ticket onboarding backlog. Which reading of the backlog is most accurate?
choices: Every first deploy still depends on a person
The backlog is a documentation problem with a quick fix available
The backlog shows that teams are filing tickets too eagerly
The backlog is a capacity problem that more headcount will solve
items.explanation: Tickets queue because the path is not self-service. More answerers shorten the wait but keep the dependency.

choices: Whether the scripts use the newest tooling available
How many engineers contributed to each script
How quickly the scripts were written by the team
Whether other teams can adopt them without help
items.explanation: Shipping a script is the product measure. Platform value is voluntary adoption and time to first deploy.

items.prompt: Payments' script took five days to write and works perfectly for Payments. A second team needs the same outcome. What is the platform move?
choices: Copy the script and edit it by hand for the second team
Ask Payments to run the second team's deploys for them
Extract what both share and parameterize the rest
Write a separate new script each time another team asks
items.explanation: The shared pattern becomes the template. Copying and per-team scripts both rebuild the bottleneck.

items.prompt: What is a paved road?
choices: A default, supported way to do a common task
A rule every team must follow to the letter
A tool that only the platform team may use
items.explanation: It is the easy default path, not a command.

items.prompt: What is an escape hatch?
choices: A backup copy of the template kept offline
A documented way to leave the paved road
A bug that lets teams skip required checks
items.explanation: It is a sanctioned, visible deviation route.

items.prompt: What does a team take on when it uses an escape hatch?
choices: The platform team's entire on-call rotation
Nothing, because the platform team still covers it
Its own upkeep for what it left behind
items.explanation: Leaving the road means owning what the road would have done.

items.prompt: Why can a mandatory road with no exit backfire?
choices: Teams deviate quietly and invisibly
Teams adopt it faster than expected
The road becomes too cheap to run
items.explanation: Hidden forks drift without the platform team knowing.

items.prompt: What does thinnest viable platform mean?
choices: Build nothing until every single team has requested it
Build the smallest thing that removes observed friction
Build the largest platform that could ever be needed
items.explanation: Start with proven friction, grow from usage.

items.prompt: Which is a good trigger to build a new golden path?
choices: An engineer guessed at a need for next year
A competitor announced a similar tool last week
Three teams each wrote near-identical setup
items.explanation: Observed repeated friction is evidence, guesses are not.

items.prompt: What should a paved road earn adoption through?
choices: Being easier than the alternative
A policy that forbids alternatives
A reward for the busiest team
items.explanation: Voluntary use is the sign it is genuinely easier.

items.prompt: Which statement about a visible exception versus a hidden fork is true?
choices: Both are equally easy to track and review
A visible exception can be reviewed later
A hidden fork is easier to manage
items.explanation: Visibility is what lets the platform team revisit it.

items.prompt: A platform team makes its CI template mandatory with no opt-out. Six months on, two teams turn out to run silent forks that were never updated. What does this show about the mandate?
choices: It removed neither the reasons to deviate nor the visibility
It kept the reasons to deviate but hid the deviations
It worked, because every team was told to use the template
It removed the reasons to deviate and the visibility of deviations
items.explanation: The mandate left the teams' real reasons intact and removed the platform team's view of what they did.
items.reference:
Road, hatch and thin start
paved road: the easy default, not a mandate
escape hatch: documented way off, owner takes upkeep
mandate with no hatch: hidden forks appear
build only for friction already observed
Why: the road wins by being easier, and a visible exit keeps deviations visible.
items.learnMore:
Paved roads need exits

A road is attractive because it is easier than the alternative. Forcing it removes the choice but not the reasons to leave, so deviations go underground where nobody sees them.

Common mistake

Treating a hidden fork as a win for consistency. The inconsistency is still there, only unobserved.
items.reflection: Think of a rule at work that people quietly route around. What would a visible, approved exception have changed?

items.prompt: A team in a regulated area needs a CI step the template cannot express. Which response keeps the platform healthiest?
choices: Grant a documented exception that names who owns the upkeep
Let them copy the template and change it without telling anyone
Rewrite the template around their one regulatory need
Refuse the request, since consistency is the platform's value
items.explanation: A recorded exception keeps visibility and ownership clear. Refusing or rewriting for one case both distort the road.

Both together, so the platform feels complete to its users
Neither one until a quarter of all teams file tickets
The pipeline template, since the friction already exists
items.explanation: Observed repeated friction beats a guess about next year.

choices: A template owned by the platform team versus one owned by its users
A template that ships with tests versus one that ships with documentation
Voluntary use with a documented way off, versus compulsory use
A fast template versus a slow template that offers more options
items.explanation: The difference is choice and visibility, not speed, ownership or test coverage.

items.prompt: Which layer is the raw cloud and clusters?
choices: Infrastructure
The portal
Golden-path templates
items.explanation: Infrastructure is the bottom layer.

items.prompt: Which layer wraps infrastructure into callable operations?
choices: The portal and catalog
Platform APIs
Golden-path templates
items.explanation: APIs turn provisioning into calls a script can make.

items.prompt: What does a golden-path template provide?
choices: Raw access to the underlying cloud accounts
A list of phone numbers for each team
Opinionated defaults built on the APIs
items.explanation: It is the preconfigured starting shape.

items.prompt: What does the service catalog record?
choices: Ownership, tier and status of services
The monthly bill from the cloud provider
Every line of code in each service
items.explanation: Ownership and status are what it answers.

items.prompt: Why do teams need a portal or catalog?
choices: To replace the version control system entirely
To find the road and see who owns what
To store nightly database backups for teams
items.explanation: Without discovery nobody knows the road exists.

items.prompt: A template waits on a human approval one layer down. Is it self-service?
choices: Yes, it looks instant to the team
Only on weekdays
No, the wait only moved down
items.explanation: The bottleneck moved, it was not removed.

items.prompt: What does a platform API replace?
choices: A ticket queue with a form on top
The source code of the team's service
The cloud provider's own control panel
items.explanation: Callable automation replaces human-processed requests.

items.prompt: Which layer would a developer touch directly in the best case?
choices: Platform APIs
The template or portal
Infrastructure
items.explanation: Developers should work at the top without needing the lower layers.

items.prompt: A scaffolding command creates a service in seconds, but the database API behind it queues requests for a manual approval. What is the most accurate description of this platform?
choices: Self-service, since the developer only runs one command
Not self-service, since the wait moved one layer below
Self-service for databases but not for the service itself
Self-service as long as approvals are answered quickly
items.explanation: Self-service must hold at every layer. A fast human is still a human on the critical path.
items.reference:
Four layers, self-service all the way down
portal and catalog: discover, see ownership
golden-path templates: opinionated defaults
platform APIs: provision, register, issue
infrastructure: cloud and clusters
Why: a human approval at any layer moves the bottleneck there, it does not remove it.
items.learnMore:
Self-service must hold at every layer

A template calls platform APIs, which call infrastructure. If any call waits for a person, the requester waits too, however polished the top looks.

Common mistake

Judging self-service by what the top layer looks like. Check the weakest layer underneath.
items.reflection: Think of a process that looks instant from the outside. Where does a hidden human step sit, and who waits for it?

items.prompt: A company offers a polished portal, but provisioning goes through a spreadsheet processed weekly by one engineer. Where should the platform team invest first?
choices: Callable platform APIs that replace the spreadsheet
A second engineer to process the spreadsheet each week
A better-looking portal for submitting requests
More documentation explaining how the spreadsheet works
items.explanation: The weak layer is the API. Polish above it and people below it leave the dependency in place.

items.prompt: What is the first step of the golden-path loop?
choices: Observe friction teams already hit
Publish the template to every team
Add guardrails to the first draft
items.explanation: Start from friction that exists.

items.prompt: After extracting a common pattern, what comes next?
choices: Delete the old scripts at once
Add guardrails and defaults
Stop and wait for more requests
items.explanation: Guardrails make the road the compliant path.

items.prompt: What does extracting a pattern mean?
choices: Removing every option from the template
Copying the first team's script unchanged
Keeping what is shared and parameterizing what varies
items.explanation: Shared parts stay, differences become parameters.

items.prompt: Which is a guardrail a template might include?
choices: A required owner tag
A longer approval chain
A random name generator
items.explanation: Required ownership data is a typical default.

items.prompt: What is golden-path coverage?
choices: How long the template takes to run in CI
How much of a team's stack the road handles
How many engineers have opened the portal this week
items.explanation: It compares road-handled work with manual work.

items.prompt: Which metric says whether the road is faster than the old way?
choices: Total number of templates in the portal
Count of pages in the internal wiki
Time to first deploy
items.explanation: It measures real speed for a new service.

items.prompt: What does tickets deflected measure?
choices: Requests the road kept off the platform team
Tickets the team managed to close overnight
Bugs that were found inside the template code
items.explanation: It shows self-service doing its job.

items.prompt: What does voluntary adoption tell you?
choices: Whether the platform team is large enough
Whether teams choose the road unforced
Whether the road costs money to maintain
items.explanation: Chosen use is the honest signal.

items.prompt: Three teams independently hand-wrote nearly identical database setup. A fourth engineer wants a template based on the first team's script, unchanged. What is the main risk?
choices: The template cannot be given a version number later
The template inherits one team's history and assumptions
The template is too general to be useful to anyone
The template will run slower than the original script did
items.explanation: Extraction means diffing and generalizing, not renaming one team's script.
items.reference:
Observe, extract, guard, publish, iterate
observe: three teams hand-write the same setup
extract: keep what is shared, parameterize the rest
guard: bake in secure defaults
measure: coverage, time to first deploy, tickets, voluntary adoption
Why: build from observed friction and keep measuring, or you ship into the dark.
items.learnMore:
From friction to template

Diff the setups, keep the shared part, parameterize what varies and drop one team's history. Add the defaults a review would demand late, then measure whether anyone adopts it.

Common mistake

Renaming the first team's script and calling it a template. It still carries that team's assumptions.
items.reflection: Think of a checklist you follow by hand every time. Which steps are the same for everyone, and which genuinely vary?

items.prompt: A published golden path shows 80 percent coverage, yet time to first deploy has not improved and tickets are flat. Which reading is most plausible?
choices: Coverage counts usage, not whether real work was removed
The measurement tools are broken and the numbers mean nothing
Coverage and speed are unrelated to each other by definition
More guardrails should be added to speed everything up
items.explanation: A road that is used but still slow suggests coverage is hiding manual steps. Compare it against time and tickets.

items.prompt: What is a service manifest?
choices: A small description of one service, filled in once
A running log of every deploy ever made
A list of every team in the company
items.explanation: It is the one hand-written input.

items.prompt: What stays out of the manifest?
choices: The service name
Facts tools can derive
The owning team
items.explanation: Derivable facts such as CI steps are computed.

items.prompt: Which tool reads the manifest to produce CI steps?
choices: The catalog search box
The billing report
The pipeline generator
items.explanation: Steps are chosen from manifest fields.

items.prompt: What does the validator answer?
choices: Whether a service meets the road's rules
How many users a service currently has
Which cloud region would be cheapest to use
items.explanation: It makes compliance machine-checkable.

items.prompt: A critical service gets which deploy style?
choices: No deploy step is added at all
Canary with automatic rollback
A plain deploy with no extra steps
items.explanation: Critical tier replaces plain deploy with canary and rollback.

items.prompt: Which field decides if a migration check is added?
choices: The programming language of the service
The name of the owner's manager
Whether the service needs a database
items.explanation: Database use triggers the migration check.

items.prompt: Why generate pipelines instead of hand-writing them?
choices: One authoritative answer, not a drifting wiki
To make the configuration files much bigger
To avoid having to use version numbers
items.explanation: Generated output cannot drift from the rule.

items.prompt: What should an escape hatch entry in a manifest contain?
choices: The full source of the change being made
A reason, an approver and an expiry
Only a short name for the hatch
items.explanation: Those make a deviation documented, not hidden.

items.prompt: A scaffolder hits an unfilled owner field in a manifest. Which behavior suits a paved-road generator best?
choices: Guess the owner from the repository's recent authors
Fail loudly or refuse to write the file
Fill in a default owner name and move on
Write the file with the placeholder left in place
items.explanation: The generator exists so nobody proofreads. Silent gaps defeat that.
items.reference:
One manifest, many readers
manifest: name, owner, tier, version, escape hatches
scaffolder, pipeline generator, validator, catalog
pipeline steps derive from tier and database use
compliant means the validator passes
Why: one hand-written input keeps every tool, and every answer, consistent.
items.learnMore:
The contract as data

When the road's rules live in a small structured file, a CI gate, a nightly audit and the portal can all run the same check. Humans stop being the compliance mechanism.

Common mistake

Duplicating derivable facts into the manifest. Anything the tools can compute should stay out of it.
items.reflection: Think of a rule your team enforces by review. Which part could be turned into data a tool checks every time?

items.prompt: Why is it better for the pipeline generator to read tier from the manifest than for each team to write its own CI?
choices: Rules such as critical services must canary are enforced, not remembered
Generated pipelines are always faster than hand-written ones
Manifests are easier to review than pipeline files
Teams are not trusted to write pipelines at all
items.explanation: Enforcement by the generator replaces a checklist someone can forget.

items.prompt: An organization stores derived facts, such as the list of CI steps, inside every manifest as well. What is the main cost?
choices: Generators will refuse to read manifests that carry extra fields
The validator can no longer check which team is the owner
The copies can drift from the generator's rules
Manifests become unreadable to anyone who is not an engineer
items.explanation: Two sources of truth disagree over time. Derive instead.
items.reference:
One manifest, many readers
manifest: name, owner, tier, version, escape hatches
scaffolder, pipeline generator, validator, catalog
pipeline steps derive from tier and database use
compliant means the validator passes
Why: one hand-written input keeps every tool, and every answer, consistent.
items.learnMore:
The contract as data

When the road's rules live in a small structured file, a CI gate, a nightly audit and the portal can all run the same check. Humans stop being the compliance mechanism.

items.prompt: What does the validator reveal about 20 services on an old template?
choices: Version drift that was invisible before
That the template is now perfect
That the catalog has no entries
items.explanation: It makes silent drift listable.

items.prompt: What makes a drift flag actionable?
choices: A longer deadline for every team
A scripted upgrade path
A louder alert sent to every channel
items.explanation: A cheap fix is what turns a flag into progress.

items.prompt: What can happen to the owner field over time?
choices: It stays correct forever on its own
It silently turns into a plain number
It becomes stale when teams disband
items.explanation: Ownership data rots unless reconciled.

items.prompt: How can ownership be kept trustworthy?
choices: Cross-check it against a live team registry
Never allow anyone to edit it again
Ask every team once a year by email
items.explanation: A periodic automatic cross-check catches mismatches.

items.prompt: Why give an escape hatch an expiry date?
choices: To delete the service
To force a revisit
To make files shorter
items.explanation: Expiry prevents permanent forks with paperwork.

items.prompt: What is a risk of generating every pipeline from one function?
choices: Teams cannot customize anything
Pipelines become identical to wikis
A bug there breaks every pipeline
items.explanation: Central code means central blast radius.

items.prompt: How should the generator itself be treated?
choices: Like any critical code, with tests
As a one-time script nobody revisits
As documentation rather than software
items.explanation: The platform needs the discipline it asks of others.

items.prompt: Does a declared escape hatch mean the deviation is resolved?
choices: Yes, it is documented
No, it still needs review
Yes, after a week has passed
items.explanation: Declared is not resolved.

items.prompt: The validator flags 20 services on a deprecated template version, but no migration tooling exists. What is the most likely outcome after three months?
choices: All 20 migrate on their own since the flag is visible
The flag becomes noise and the services stay put
The deprecated version stops working automatically
The validator is switched off by its owners
items.explanation: Visibility without a cheap upgrade path produces a backlog nobody schedules.
items.reference:
Checking is not fixing
version drift: a flag needs a scripted upgrade
ownership rot: cross-check a live team registry
escape hatches: expiry dates force a revisit
generator bug: breaks every pipeline at once
Why: visibility is step one; a cheap fix path and periodic review keep the numbers shrinking.
items.learnMore:
Why checks decay

Every check that flags a problem without a cheap fix becomes noise. Pair each check with an upgrade path, an owner and a review rhythm.

Common mistake

Treating a flag as the end of the job. A list of 20 stale services is a backlog, not a solution.
